articles.title: Federal budget names Calgary projects as Ottawa projects a $62.3-billion deficit
articles.dek: Budget 2026, tabled Thursday, lists a Calgary community centre and a defence quantum hub, and puts major federal transfers to Alberta at $9.2 billion next year.
body: The federal government tabled Budget 2026 on Thursday, projecting a deficit of $62.3 billion for 2026-27. It forecasts revenue of $540.3 billion and expenses of $602.9 billion before actuarial changes, with federal debt at 39.9% of GDP [1]. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne presented the budget, which carries the title "Masters of our destiny" [2].

Calgary appears by name in two places. The list of projects the budget proposes to support through the Build Communities Strong Fund includes the Silver Springs Community Centre building expansion in Calgary, alongside two Edmonton projects [3]. The budget describes the fund as $51 billion over 10 years starting in 2026-27, and $3 billion a year after that [3]. The defence chapter notes that the Quantum Defence Innovation Secure Hub, part of the BOREALIS defence innovation program, was launched in Calgary [4].

Elsewhere in Alberta, the defence chapter lists future fighter capabilities at CFB Cold Lake, a chemical and biological laboratory and blast assessment centre at CFB Suffield, a western operating base for the Royal Canadian Air Force's CC-330 Husky fleet, and maintenance work across Alberta bases. It also proposes $25 million over two years and $3 million for the military family resource centre at CFB Wainwright after a deadly training incident there [4].
Three Alberta projects appear on the budget's list of projects referred to the federal Major Projects Office: Alberta High-Speed Rail, the Pacific Link Pipeline and Pathways Plus [5].

Finance Canada's transfer tables put Alberta's Canada Health Transfer at $7.04 billion and its Canada Social Transfer at $2.20 billion in 2026-27, a total of $9.24 billion, or $1,792 per resident. That is up from $8.71 billion in 2025-26. Alberta receives no equalization payment [6].

Several national measures reach households in every province, including Calgary. The budget proposes a one-time 2027 supplement to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which it costs at $4.1 billion, and notes that the federal fuel excise tax relief has been extended to the end of January 2027, with rates restored to half their usual level until the end of March [3].
The Calgary Data Desk's Federal Budget 2026 section lists every measure in the budget, with its cost by year, and what the budget names in each province.
key_facts: Silver Springs Community Centre expansion named under the Build Communities Strong Fund
Major transfers to Alberta 2026-27: $9.24 billion ($1,792 per person)

articles.title: Committee backs a pause on large data centre applications; council to debate
articles.dek: City council's executive committee voted 10-3 for a notice of motion seeking a temporary moratorium on land-use applications for large-scale data centres.
body: Calgary's executive committee on Tuesday approved, by a 10-3 vote, a notice of motion that would temporarily freeze new land-use redesignation applications for large-scale data centres. The motion now goes to a full meeting of city council for debate [1]. Reports have not given a date for that debate [4].

The motion is sponsored by Mayor Jeromy Farkas and councillors Jennifer Wyness (Ward 2), Raj Dhaliwal (Ward 5), Andrew Yule and John Pantazopoulos (Ward 6) [1][2]. It asks city administration to report by March 2027 on changes to the land use bylaw, including a definition of data centres at different scales, and to return by the end of 2027 with a study of their risks and opportunities, including environmental impacts and the effect on regional and municipal water servicing [2][3].

Sponsors pointed to unanswered questions about water consumption, electricity use, stormwater and wastewater needs and noise, and to concerns that utility bills could rise [3]. Pantazopoulos described the pause as 12 months on new redesignations for data centres [3]. Farkas said the city should regulate artificial intelligence data centres so Calgary does not become a "Wild West" [1]. The motion separates small and medium data centres, which it says resemble other commercial and industrial users, from hyperscale artificial intelligence and cloud campuses [2].

Rocky View County, Saskatoon, Mississauga and Oakville have already adopted similar pauses [1][2]. Ward 8 Coun. Nathaniel Schmidt said he supports the motion and wants the province to take a more active role [1]. The provincial government's House Leader has said its fall legislative agenda includes protections for data centre development, though details have not been released [1].

One application already in the system, LOC2026-0156, would redesignate undeveloped land east of 52 Street N.E. and north of Redstone to allow large industrial buildings, power generation and a data centre. It remains under review and continues through the city's process [1][2][3].

articles.title: Stage 4 water restrictions in effect while crews connect the new Bearspaw feeder main
articles.dek: All outdoor water use is banned for about four weeks, and the City is asking residents to help keep daily use under 500 million litres.
body: Stage 4 water restrictions took effect across Calgary on Wednesday, Nov. 4. The Bearspaw South Feeder Main is shut down for about four weeks while crews connect the new replacement pipe to the existing system. During the work, the Glenmore treatment plant supplies roughly 80% of the water for the city and region [1].

Under Stage 4, outdoor water use is prohibited, including watering lawns, gardens and trees, washing driveways, sidewalks and cars on the street, construction water use, filling pools and hot tubs, and outdoor snow or ice making, which rules out flooding backyard rinks [1][2]. Exceptions include indoor car washes and hand-watering edible crops [1]. Fines start at $3,000 [1].

Indoors, the City is asking residents to run dishwashers and washing machines only with full loads, flush only when needed, keep showers to about three minutes and fix leaks [1]. The aim is to keep daily demand below 500 million litres. Above that level, the City says, the system risks not having enough water for firefighting, low pressure, a possible boil water advisory or a treatment failure [1].
The restrictions also apply in communities served by Calgary's system: Airdrie, Chestermere, Strathmore and the Tsuut'ina Nation [3].

Crews are draining the pipe, cutting the existing main and installing custom pieces to join the new pipe, followed by welding, backfilling and water quality testing [2]. Commissioning is expected to run until mid-December, and the City expects the new feeder main to be fully operating by the end of 2026 [2][3]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas called the 11-month project a significant milestone and asked Calgarians to cooperate one more time [2]. Questions go to 311 [1].
key_facts: In effect from Nov. 4 for about four weeks
Daily use target: under 500 million litres

articles.title: House fire and explosion near Okotoks closes a nearby high school
articles.dek: Foothills County firefighters responded to a rural property near Heritage Heights School on Thursday morning; early reports said no one was believed hurt.
body: Emergency crews responded to a house fire and explosion at a rural property in Foothills County, southeast of Calgary near Okotoks, on Thursday morning. Reports began coming in shortly after 7 a.m., and photos and videos of the fire circulated online [1][2].

The property is near Heritage Heights School, which closed for the day as a precaution. Students who arrive by bus were taken to École Percy Pegler in Okotoks, where parents could pick them up [1][2]. The area around the property was evacuated [2]. A resident of nearby Heritage Pointe described the blast as feeling like a bomb going off [1].

The Foothills County fire department handled the call. The Calgary Fire Department sent a crew from its Seton station but stood it down because the property is outside city limits; a department spokesperson said the county's crews did not need Calgary's help [1][2].

No one was believed to have been hurt, though that had not been confirmed, and officials had not given a cause for the fire or the explosion [1]. CTV News described the story as developing, with updates through the morning [3].
key_facts: Heritage Heights School closed for the day
